transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, thank you for seeing me. I... I really didn't know where else to turn at this point. You know, I'm 65 now, I'm not working anymore, so my days are mostly my own and usually pretty quiet, but... well, I came in today because things have just gotten so out of hand behind closed doors. 

It's these nights. These awful nights of eating. When it's all over, I just sit there in my chair, and I look around, and there are just crumbs everywhere. Just crumbs and empty containers and wrappers all around me on the coffee table and the floor. And I sit in the middle of that mess and I feel so... so incredibly ashamed. Just absolutely disgusted with myself. It's this heavy, horrible feeling that just washes over me and stays there, weighing me down. 

It gets so bad that the next morning, I can barely even bring myself to pray. I get dressed and go to church, because that's what I've always done, but when I get there... I can hardly look folks in the eye. I just keep my head down the whole service. I feel like they can all see right through me, like they know what a failure I am and what I was doing the night before in my living room. It's just tearing me apart, sitting there in the pews feeling so dirty and out of control, and I just... I can't keep living with this kind of shame every week.
Do you usually feel stressed, anxious, or upset before these nights of eating?

You know, doctor, I've asked myself that very same question a hundred times. I'll sit in my chair the next day and try to retrace my steps, almost like a detective or something, trying to figure out what exactly set me off. But... honestly? No, I wouldn't say I feel stressed or upset before it starts. I'm really not sure that I feel much of anything. 

I mean, what do I really have to be stressed about these days? I'm 65, I'm not working anymore, the house is paid for, and my time is just my own. Most of the time, the house is perfectly quiet. I might just be sitting there in the evening, watching my programs—I always watch Jeopardy and Wheel of Fortune, it's just a little routine I have to pass the time—and I'll be feeling completely fine. Just... ordinary. Not anxious, not crying, not worried about a bill or anything in particular. I'll just be sitting there, maybe doing a little cross-stitch or just looking out the window as it gets dark, and I don't feel upset at all. 

I really wish I could tell you that I was having a panic attack or feeling terribly sad right before I go to the pantry, because then it would make sense, wouldn't it? Then I could point to it and say, "Aha, that's why I did it." But I really haven't noticed feeling anything like that beforehand. I'm just going about my quiet evening, and then... I just find myself in the kitchen. So no, I wouldn't say stress or being upset has anything to do with it, as far as I can tell.
Do you feel like you have to eat when you're in the kitchen, like you can't stop yourself once you've started?

Yes... yes, that's exactly it. It's the strangest, most frightening thing, doctor. I'll just be standing there in the kitchen, and maybe the refrigerator hum is the only sound in the whole house because, like I said, it gets so very quiet in the evenings. And I'll open a cabinet, just looking, maybe thinking I'll have one little cracker. Just one. 

But... once I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense just completely steps aside. It just walks right out the door. I'll be standing there, and my mind is perfectly clear in a way, because I'm actually talking to myself. I'm standing right there on the linoleum in my slippers, and I'm telling myself, "Belinda, stop now. You don't need this, Belinda, just put the box down and go back to your chair." I say it over and over in my head. I'm practically pleading with myself. 

But it's like my body doesn't even hear me. My hands just keep reaching for more. I'll finish one thing, and before I've even swallowed, my hand is already in another box, pulling out cookies or crackers or whatever is sitting on the shelf. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body, just watching my hands do all this work, tearing open wrappers and reaching and reaching. I want to stop, I really do, but I just can't seem to make my hands listen to my brain once that first bite goes past my lips. I just keep going and going, even while I'm telling myself how foolish it is.
Do you feel like you're in control of what you're eating during these episodes?

Well, no, doctor, I don't. Not at all. I know I just touched on this a moment ago, but it really is the crux of the whole miserable thing, isn't it? Control. Or the complete lack of it, I should say. 

It's like I was just trying to explain... once I take that very first bite, usually right after Jeopardy is over and the house has gotten so still and quiet... it's like my good sense just steps aside entirely. It's the most bizarre feeling. I'll be standing there, and I know exactly what I'm doing, and I'm practically having a full conversation with myself in my head. I'm saying, "Belinda, stop now. You don't need this, Belinda, just put the box down and go back to your chair." I'll say it over and over, clear as a bell. 

But it doesn't matter what I say to myself. It's like my hands have a mind of their own. They just keep reaching for more, opening another box, tearing into another bag, and I'm just standing there watching it happen. I'm completely aware of how ridiculous it is, how much I'm going to hate myself in the morning when I'm sitting in church, but I just can't stop it. The control is just... gone. It's completely gone the second that first crumb touches my tongue. I don't know how else to describe it, it's just like I'm entirely powerless over my own hands.
Is the shame you feel after these episodes more because of the amount you've eaten or because you felt like you couldn't control your actions?

Well, doctor, I suppose it’s... it’s a little bit of both, really, but they’re so tangled up together it’s hard to pull them apart. It’s the amount, yes, because when it’s all over, I’ll look down at the counter, and there will be all these empty wrappers and boxes and crumbs just everywhere. I mean, it’s a mess. And I’ll look at it and think, "How could one person eat all of this in one sitting?" It’s just staggering. 

But I think the real weight of it, the part that just settles right in my chest and makes it hard to breathe, is the control part. Or the lack of it, like we just talked about. It’s the fact that I knew I was doing it, and I wanted to stop, and I just couldn't. That’s where the disgust really comes in. I mean, I’m a 65-year-old woman. I should be able to tell myself "no" and have it stick. 

And that’s really why I came to see you, doctor. Because after these nights, I’ll just sit there in the kitchen, staring at the crumbs and the empty containers, and I feel so... so deeply ashamed. I feel so disgusted with myself that it just lingers. It hangs over me like a dark cloud. I’ll wake up the next morning, usually on a Sunday, and I’ll try to get ready for church, but I can hardly even bring myself to pray. I just feel so unworthy, so out of control. And then I’ll go to the service, and I’ll be sitting in my usual pew, and I can hardly look folks in the eye. I just keep my head down, thinking they must somehow know what a mess I am, what I did the night before when no one was looking. It’s just an awful, heavy feeling to carry around, doctor, and I just can’t keep living with this kind of shame every time the house gets quiet.
Does this feeling of losing control happen to you with things other than eating?

Oh, no... no, doctor, it really doesn't. And that’s the strangest part of it all, if I'm being perfectly honest. I am actually a very... well, a very disciplined person in just about every other area of my life. 

I mean, I keep a very strict budget. Living on a fixed income these days, you really have to, you know? Every single penny is accounted for. I sit down at the kitchen table—the exact same table where all this... this awful mess happens later on—every Tuesday morning with my checkbook and a cup of decaf, and I make sure everything balances down to the dime. I don't go out and buy things I don't need. I don't gamble, I don't even drink anything stronger than iced tea. I keep my home tidy, everything has its proper place, and my flower beds out front are always weeded by Friday afternoon before the weekend. I like order, doctor. I really do. I like things to be predictable and manageable. 

So, no, I don't lose control like that with anything else. I can walk right past a big sale at the department store and not even bat an eye. I can tell myself "no" about buying a new pair of shoes or a new handbag, and it's perfectly fine. The "no" sticks. I don't even think twice about it. 

But then... then the evening comes, and I'm standing there in my slippers, looking at a sleeve of cookies or a box of Ritz crackers, and all that discipline, all that careful planning and control I maintain all day long... it just evaporates. It's only the food. And I just don't understand why I can be so sensible and strict about my checkbook and my garden, but I can't seem to apply that exact same good sense to my own pantry. It makes absolutely no sense to me.
Does this loss of control happen with any other activities besides eating?

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, doctor, no. It really doesn't. I know we just touched on that, but it truly is just the eating. I don't have any other bad habits where I just let go of the reins like that. 

I don't sit in front of the television ordering things I don't need off QVC, and I don't hoard things in the garage. I mean, my garage is swept clean every first of the month, you could practically eat off the floor out there. And I don't lose my temper with people, either. You know, some folks lose control of their emotions, they yell at the poor cashier at the grocery store or they honk their horns and carry on in traffic. Not me. I'm always the one keeping the peace, always very level-headed. Just last week, Mrs. Higgins down the street let her little terrier dig up my marigolds—the ones I just told you I keep so nicely weeded—and did I scream and shout? No, I just calmly went over and had a very polite, measured word with her about it. 

So I really do have a very firm grip on myself in every single other aspect of my day-to-day life. I am a sensible woman. It's just... it's just the pantry. It's just when the sun goes down and I'm alone in the house with the food. That's the absolute only time that switch flips in my brain and I just completely lose my grip on myself. So, no, to answer your question again, it doesn't happen with absolutely anything else at all. Just the food.
Do you think the loss of control with eating happens because you're feeling a certain way, like bored, lonely, or something else, when you're alone in the house at night?

Well, I suppose... yes, I suppose there is something to that, doctor. It’s the quiet, you see. When the house is just so still. And it’s not just that I’m alone, because I’ve been alone in this house since my husband passed away seven years ago, and I never used to do this. I’d knit, or read a book, or listen to the radio. I was perfectly content with my own company. 

But this... this whole terrible business with the eating, this complete unraveling of my self-control in the evenings, it only started recently. It’s been going on for about five months now. Exactly five months, actually, if I think about it. 

You see, five months ago... oh, it’s hard to even talk about it without getting a little choked up. Five months ago, my dearest friend, Martha, passed away. We were closer than sisters, doctor. We played bridge every Thursday afternoon for twenty years, right at that same kitchen table I was telling you about. And we sat next to each other in church every single Sunday. We were the ones who organized the bake sales, the ones who always stayed late to fold the bulletins. When you get to be my age, the friends you have left, the ones who really know you, who remember you when you were young... they become your whole world. 

And then she had a stroke, just out of the blue. One day we were having tea and talking about the pastor’s sermon, and three days later she was gone. Just gone. And ever since then... well, that’s when this started. I’d come home from the funeral, and the house just felt so empty. Not just quiet, but... hollow. Like all the air had been let out of it. And that’s when I first found myself in the pantry, just eating crackers without even tasting them. I suppose I was lonely, yes. More than lonely, really. I was just... adrift. And I’ve been adrift for five months now, trying to fill up this awful quiet with... with whatever I can find in the cupboards. So yes, I think you’re right. I think it’s exactly how I’m feeling when I’m alone in that house.
Do you feel like you're compelled to continue eating once you start, even if you don't want to?

Oh, compelled... yes, that's exactly the word for it, doctor. Compelled. It’s the most frightening feeling, really, because as I was just telling you, I am a woman who prides herself on being in charge of her own actions. I like to be the one steering the ship, so to speak. 

But once I am standing there in the kitchen—usually right by the counter where I keep the toaster, because I don't even bother to sit down at the table anymore when this happens—once I take that very first bite after the house gets all quiet... it's like my good sense just completely steps aside. It just packs its bags and walks right out the back door. 

I’ll be standing there, and my brain is fully awake, mind you. I'm not in a daze or asleep. I am literally standing there telling myself, sometimes even out loud in the empty kitchen, "Belinda, stop now. You don't need this. You aren't even hungry, Belinda." I say it just like that, using my own name, like I'm scolding a child who is reaching for the cookie jar before supper. I try to be firm with myself. 

But it doesn't matter. It doesn't matter one bit what I say to myself, because my hands... my hands just keep reaching for more. It's like they belong to somebody else entirely. I'll watch my own hand reach into the box, pull out another handful, and bring it to my mouth, and I'm thinking, "Why are you doing this?" but I just keep chewing and swallowing and reaching again. The compulsion is so terribly strong, it's like a heavy wave that just washes over all my good intentions and all my strict rules. I just can't seem to make my hands listen to my head once that first bite goes past my lips.
Do you think you lose control over eating when you're feeling emotional, such as sad or anxious, rather than just when you're alone in the house?

Well, I suppose... I suppose I don't really know, doctor. I mean, I know I just told you about how sad I've been since Martha passed, and how the house feels so empty, but... is it the sadness making me eat, or just the fact that I'm alone in the quiet? I honestly couldn't tell you where one ends and the other begins. 

It's all sort of tangled up together now, isn't it? Because when I'm alone, I feel sad, and when I'm sad, I'm usually alone. I don't really go out much anymore, not since she died. I used to go to the grocery store on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and maybe stop by the pharmacy, but now I just go once a week, very quickly, just to get it over with. So I'm in the house a lot more. And when I'm in the house, I'm alone. And when I'm alone, I think about her, and I think about how things used to be, and I get that awful hollow feeling in my chest. 

But do I lose control *because* I'm sad, or just because nobody is there to see me? If someone were sitting right there in the living room with me, even if I was feeling terribly low, I wouldn't go into the pantry and eat a whole sleeve of crackers and a jar of peanut butter. I just wouldn't. I have too much pride for that. I would offer them a cup of tea, like a proper hostess, and we would sit and talk. 

So it's the being alone that allows it to happen, if that makes sense. But the sadness... the sadness is always there now, humming in the background like a refrigerator. So I really can't say for sure if it's the emotion or the isolation. I just know that when it's evening, and it's quiet, and it's just me... that's when the wheels come off. I'm sorry I can't give you a more precise answer, doctor. It's just all very confusing to me, to be honest. I never used to be a confused person. I always knew exactly why I did things. But this... this is different.
Do you think you would lose control over eating if you were feeling sad or anxious, but not alone?

Oh, heavens no. No, I wouldn't do that. I couldn't possibly do that, doctor. If there were people around... no matter how sad or anxious or completely dreadful I was feeling inside, I would never, ever let myself go like that in front of an audience. It’s just... well, it’s a matter of dignity, isn’t it? A matter of how one presents oneself to the world. 

I’ve always been very particular about that, you see. Even now, with everything that's happened, I still try to keep up appearances. Take the church suppers, for instance, or when the ladies still try to get a bridge game together without Martha... bless their hearts for trying, but it’s just not the same. Anyway, when I go to those gatherings, I make an absolute point of taking just a modest little plate. A very sensible portion. A small scoop of the ambrosia salad, maybe one dinner roll, a tiny slice of ham. I sit there and I eat delicately, like a bird, and I chat, and I make sure everyone sees that Belinda is doing just fine, that she’s keeping it all together. 

But then... oh, it’s so shameful to even admit this. Then, after everyone has gone home, or after I’ve brought a covered dish back to my own house... that’s when it happens. I wait until I am completely alone, until the door is locked and the blinds are drawn, and I pull those leftovers right out in the kitchen. I don't even put them on a proper plate most of the time. I just stand there where nobody on earth can see me, and I eat, and I eat, and I eat until I feel sick. Because if anyone ever saw me doing that... if any of the ladies from the altar guild ever saw me shoveling food into my mouth like a... like a starving animal, well, I think I would just die of embarrassment on the spot. I truly would. The thought of them seeing me lose control like that, no matter how sad I am... it’s just unbearable. So no, doctor, I have to be alone. I have to hide it.
Do you think you would eat excessively if you were feeling very anxious or stressed, even if you weren't alone?

Well, doctor, I know I just touched on this a moment ago, but I really can't emphasize enough how impossible that would be for me. The answer is absolutely not. Never. It truly wouldn't matter if I were stressed to the absolute breaking point—and frankly, I *do* get very anxious sometimes at these gatherings now. Going to the church suppers or sitting down at those bridge games without Martha... it's incredibly stressful. The other ladies, bless them, they hover, and they ask so many probing questions about how I'm coping, and my heart just races and my stomach ties itself into awful little knots. I feel so much anxiety in those moments I could just scream. 

But even then, even with all that stress making my hands shake, I do exactly what I just told you. I make a strict point of taking a modest little plate. I'll smile and take one little scoop of casserole, or just half a deviled egg, and I sit there making polite conversation while I'm just churning with nerves on the inside. I will not let them see me crack, and I certainly won't let them see me eat my feelings, so to speak. 

It's only later, you see. The stress doesn't go away, it just waits for an audience of one. So after the event is over, and everyone has finally gone home to their own families, and I've driven myself back to my empty house... that is when the dam breaks. I take whatever leftovers I brought back with me, and I pull them right out in the kitchen where absolutely nobody can see me. That's when I eat, and eat, and eat. I have to be completely hidden away from the world, because the embarrassment of someone seeing me use food to cope with my stress... well, it would ruin me. I just couldn't survive the shame of it. So I hold it all in, all that anxiety, until I am safely standing in my own kitchen, completely out of sight.
Do you think the loss of control with eating happens because you're feeling emotional, such as sad or lonely, when you're by yourself?

Yes, I suppose that is exactly it, doctor. It’s the combination of the two, isn't it? The heavy emotions and the empty house, mixing together like a terrible recipe. 

You see, during the day, the daylight somehow keeps the worst of the loneliness at bay. I can look out the window and see the neighbor, Mr. Henderson, walking his golden retriever, or the mail carrier dropping off the post. But when the sun goes down... oh, the house just gets so terribly, awfully quiet. You can hear the grandfather clock ticking all the way from the hallway, and every single tick just reminds me that I'm completely alone in the world now. The loneliness just washes over me like a cold draft. I try to distract myself, I truly do. I'll turn on the television, maybe try to watch a bit of Jeopardy, or I'll pick up my knitting—I'm working on a lovely pastel yellow blanket for my niece's new baby—but the sadness is just sitting right there next to me on the sofa, thick and heavy.

And then, before I even fully realize what I'm doing, I end up in the kitchen. It's almost like I just drift in there to escape the silence in the living room. And... well, once I take the first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense steps aside. I don't know where it goes, but it just vanishes completely. It is the strangest, most frightening feeling, because even while I'm telling myself, right there in my own head, 'Belinda, stop now, you're going to make yourself miserable,' my hands keep reaching for more. 

I’ll just stand there at the counter, and I tell my brain to tell my hands to put the package down, to close the pantry door, to just walk away. I am a sensible woman, doctor. I balance my own checkbook, I keep a spotless house, I know how to behave. But in those moments, with that awful sadness pressing down on me and nobody around to see... my brain just disconnects from my body. My hands just keep going back for another bite, and another, and another, completely ignoring my own instructions to stop. It’s as if someone else is driving the car, if you know what I mean.
Do you think you would experience a loss of control with eating if you were feeling angry or frustrated, rather than sad or lonely?

Well, doctor, anger... yes, frustration too. It really doesn't seem to matter what the awful feeling is, to be perfectly honest with you. 

Just this past Tuesday, for instance, I was on the telephone with the electric company—and oh, please don't even get me started on them, they sent me a billing notice that made absolutely no sense whatsoever, and the young girl on the customer service line was so incredibly dismissive. She kept reading from a script, treating me like I didn't know how to read my own meter. I was just boiling over by the time I finally slammed the receiver down. I was pacing the hallway, just fuming, my heart going a mile a minute. 

And there I was, all worked up, and the house was just... well, it was dead quiet, just like I was saying before. And that frustration just bubbled up and pushed me right into the kitchen. 

And it's exactly that same terrifying feeling I was just trying to explain to you. It truly doesn't matter if I'm crying from loneliness or if I'm just mad as a hornet at the electric company. The very second I take that first bite in that silent house, my good sense just packs up and walks right out the door. It completely steps aside. I was standing there at the counter with a whole tin of shortbread cookies, and I was so angry, and my brain was practically screaming at me, 'Belinda, stop now, this isn't going to fix the electric bill, you are being ridiculous!' 

But my hands... it's like they didn't even hear me. They just kept reaching into that tin for more. I was so angry at that girl on the phone, and then I was instantly angry at myself because I couldn't stop my own fingers from grabbing another cookie, and another, and another. I’ll be chewing and swallowing and literally begging myself to just put the lid back on the tin and walk away, maybe go water the African violets or do something, anything, productive. But I just can't. The feeling of losing command over my own body... it happens with the frustration just as much as the sadness. It really is a dreadful cycle, doctor. I just don't know how I let myself get to this point where a simple phone call can send me into such a state where I can't even control my own hands.
Can you think of any instances where you lost control over eating when you were feeling happy or excited, rather than sad, lonely, or frustrated?

Well, doctor, you would think that wouldn't happen, wouldn't you? You would think that being happy or having a wonderful day would be enough to keep me out of the pantry. I certainly used to think so. But... oh dear, I'm afraid the answer is yes. It happens then, too. 

Just last month, for example, my niece—the one I mentioned earlier, the one I'm knitting that yellow blanket for—she called me on a Sunday afternoon to tell me they had finally settled on a name for the baby. Oh, I was just over the moon! She told me they're going to name her Eleanor, after my late mother. Well, I was practically in tears, good tears, just so completely thrilled and honored. We must have talked for an hour about the nursery and the baby clothes. 

When we finally hung up, I was just floating. I walked into the kitchen to make myself a nice cup of Earl Grey tea to sort of celebrate, you know? Just basking in the good news. But then... well, the phone was back on the hook, and suddenly the house was just so terribly quiet again. All that wonderful excitement was bubbling up inside me, but there was absolutely no one sitting in the kitchen with me to share it with. 

I opened the cupboard just to get a single biscuit to have with my tea. Just one. But doctor, I know I sound like a broken record today, but it is exactly what I was trying to explain to you before. It really doesn't matter if it's good news or bad news. Once I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside. It simply evaporates. 

I was standing there, feeling so joyful about little baby Eleanor, and yet... I went through the entire package of cookies. And then a whole box of graham crackers. And even while I'm standing there, telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now, you’re having such a wonderful day, please don’t ruin it,' my hands just keep reaching for more. They just keep going. It’s as if the loss of control doesn't care whether I'm crying or cheering. The minute I take that first bite in an empty house, my brain and my hands just stop talking to each other completely. It’s just so exhausting, doctor, to not even be able to celebrate a beautiful thing without... without turning into this person I don't even recognize.
Do you think you would experience a loss of control with eating if you were feeling a strong emotional state, such as excitement or euphoria, when you're alone?

Well, doctor, as I was just saying about the wonderful news with little baby Eleanor... that was pure euphoria! I was absolutely beside myself with joy. But yes, to answer your question, it is still exactly the same result. It really doesn't matter if it's the highest high or the lowest low, you see. 

I could be on top of the world—maybe I just won the sweepstakes or found out I was going on a luxury cruise. Not that I play the sweepstakes, mind you, I've always thought they were a bit of a scam, my late husband Arthur used to say that all the time, bless his heart. But if I were completely euphoric like that, and I came back to my house and there was no one there to share it with... oh, it wouldn't make a lick of difference. The silence just amplifies the emotion, whatever it happens to be, until it's just buzzing under my skin. 

Like I've been trying to explain, it all comes back to being alone in that empty house. Once I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside completely. It just vanishes into thin air! And it is so incredibly frustrating, because even while I'm standing right there by the pantry, telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now, you don't need to do this,' my hands just keep reaching for more. My brain is giving the sensible orders, but my hands just absolutely refuse to listen. It’s like the euphoria itself just short-circuits my body the second the front door clicks shut and I'm by myself.
Do you think you would lose control over eating if you were alone but in a neutral emotional state, without feeling particularly sad, angry, or excited?

Well doctor, it is funny you should ask that. Because just an ordinary Thursday... I think it was last Thursday, yes, because the garbage truck had just come by, and they always make such a racket out on the street. After they left, I was just doing my regular chores. Dusting the credenza my late husband Arthur built, folding some hand towels, nothing special at all. I wasn't sad, I wasn't happy, I certainly wasn't angry like I was with the electric company. I was just going about my business, feeling perfectly fine and normal, just a regular day. 

I went into the kitchen to have a little snack before my afternoon television programs came on. And I know I must sound like a broken record to you by now, I really do, but I have to tell you, it is the exact same story. It does not need a big, powerful emotion to start the whole dreadful thing. It is just the silence. The house gets so terribly quiet again after the chores are done. 

I know I have said this to you three times already, but it is the honest truth, the very moment I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it is like my good sense just completely steps aside. It just checks out! I will be standing right there by the counter, looking at a bag of pretzels or a box of crackers, and I am telling myself in my head, Belinda, stop now, you are not even upset, you are just bored, put the bag away. But my hands just keep reaching for more. They simply do not listen to a single word I am thinking. 

It is the most baffling thing in the world, doctor. You would think without the sadness or the excitement pushing me, I would be able to just put the food down and go read a magazine or do a crossword puzzle. But no, the quiet just settles in, and I lose all command all over again, even on a perfectly boring, ordinary afternoon. It is like my hands have a mind of their own, and they just keep going and going until everything is gone, no matter how I am feeling inside.
Do you think you would lose control over eating if you were alone but feeling completely neutral emotionally?

Well, doctor, did... did I not just answer that? Oh dear, perhaps I didn't explain it clearly enough, or maybe I just rambled on too much and lost the thread. My late husband, Arthur, always did say I could talk the ear off a brass monkey if you let me. But yes, to be perfectly clear, if I am completely and utterly neutral—just absolutely nothing going on in my head, maybe just standing at the sink watching the neighbor's cat, Mr. Whiskers, walk along the back fence—it still happens. It happens exactly the same way. 

Like I was just saying about doing my chores last Thursday, you really cannot find a more neutral feeling than folding hand towels. I wasn't feeling a single thing. But the house is still so terribly empty. And I know I keep repeating myself to you today, I really do, but it is the absolute gospel truth: once I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside. It just takes a holiday! And even while I'm standing right there in the middle of the kitchen, looking at whatever it is I've opened, and telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now, you aren't even upset, you don't even want this,' my hands just keep reaching for more. 

They just keep reaching and reaching, completely ignoring my brain. doctor.question: Do you think you would experience a loss of control with eating if you were feeling angry or frustrated, rather than sad or lonely?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I take the first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense steps aside, and even while I'm telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands keep reaching for more.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the loss of control over eating occurs with other emotions like anger or frustration, which directly relates to the symptom of experiencing a lack of control during eating episodes.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, anger... yes, frustration too. It really doesn't seem to matter what the awful feeling is, to be perfectly honest with you. 

Just this past Tuesday, for instance, I was on the telephone with the electric company—and oh, please don't even get me started on them, they sent me a billing notice that made absolutely no sense whatsoever, and the young girl on the customer service line was so incredibly dismissive. She kept reading from a script, treating me like I didn't know how to read my own meter. I was just boiling over by the time I finally slammed the receiver down. I was pacing the hallway, just fuming, my heart going a mile a minute. 

And there I was, all worked up, and the house was just... well, it was dead quiet, just like I was saying before. And that frustration just bubbled up and pushed me right into the kitchen. 

And it's exactly that same terrifying feeling I was just trying to explain to you. It truly doesn't matter if I'm crying from loneliness or if I'm just mad as a hornet at the electric company. The very second I take that first bite in that silent house, my good sense just packs up and walks right out the door. It completely steps aside. I was standing there at the counter with a whole tin of shortbread cookies, and I was so angry, and my brain was practically screaming at me, 'Belinda, stop now, this isn't going to fix the electric bill, you are being ridiculous!' 

But my hands... it's like they didn't even hear me. They just kept reaching into that tin for more. I was so angry at that girl on the phone, and then I was instantly angry at myself because I couldn't stop my own fingers from grabbing another cookie, and another, and another. I’ll be chewing and swallowing and literally begging myself to just put the lid back on the tin and walk away, maybe go water the African violets or do something, anything, productive. But I just can't. The feeling of losing command over my own body... it happens with the frustration just as much as the sadness. It really is a dreadful cycle, doctor. I just don't know how I let myself get to this point where a simple phone call can send me into such a state where I can't even control my own hands.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's loss of control with eating is specifically related to emotional states such as sadness or loneliness, or if it can be triggered by other emotional states as well
doctor.question: Can you think of any instances where you lost control over eating when you were feeling happy or excited, rather than sad, lonely, or frustrated?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I take the first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense steps aside, and even while I'm telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands keep reaching for more.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about experiencing a loss of control over eating in different emotional states (happy or excited), which directly relates to the symptom of Loss of Control.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, you would think that wouldn't happen, wouldn't you? You would think that being happy or having a wonderful day would be enough to keep me out of the pantry. I certainly used to think so. But... oh dear, I'm afraid the answer is yes. It happens then, too. 

Just last month, for example, my niece—the one I mentioned earlier, the one I'm knitting that yellow blanket for—she called me on a Sunday afternoon to tell me they had finally settled on a name for the baby. Oh, I was just over the moon! She told me they're going to name her Eleanor, after my late mother. Well, I was practically in tears, good tears, just so completely thrilled and honored. We must have talked for an hour about the nursery and the baby clothes. 

When we finally hung up, I was just floating. I walked into the kitchen to make myself a nice cup of Earl Grey tea to sort of celebrate, you know? Just basking in the good news. But then... well, the phone was back on the hook, and suddenly the house was just so terribly quiet again. All that wonderful excitement was bubbling up inside me, but there was absolutely no one sitting in the kitchen with me to share it with. 

I opened the cupboard just to get a single biscuit to have with my tea. Just one. But doctor, I know I sound like a broken record today, but it is exactly what I was trying to explain to you before. It really doesn't matter if it's good news or bad news. Once I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside. It simply evaporates. 

I was standing there, feeling so joyful about little baby Eleanor, and yet... I went through the entire package of cookies. And then a whole box of graham crackers. And even while I'm standing there, telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now, you’re having such a wonderful day, please don’t ruin it,' my hands just keep reaching for more. They just keep going. It’s as if the loss of control doesn't care whether I'm crying or cheering. The minute I take that first bite in an empty house, my brain and my hands just stop talking to each other completely. It’s just so exhausting, doctor, to not even be able to celebrate a beautiful thing without... without turning into this person I don't even recognize.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's loss of control over eating is related to emotional states other than sadness or loneliness
doctor.question: Do you think you would experience a loss of control with eating if you were feeling a strong emotional state, such as excitement or euphoria, when you're alone?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I take the first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense steps aside, and even while I'm telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands keep reaching for more.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking again about experiencing a loss of control over eating, specifically in the context of strong emotional states like excitement or euphoria.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, as I was just saying about the wonderful news with little baby Eleanor... that was pure euphoria! I was absolutely beside myself with joy. But yes, to answer your question, it is still exactly the same result. It really doesn't matter if it's the highest high or the lowest low, you see. 

I could be on top of the world—maybe I just won the sweepstakes or found out I was going on a luxury cruise. Not that I play the sweepstakes, mind you, I've always thought they were a bit of a scam, my late husband Arthur used to say that all the time, bless his heart. But if I were completely euphoric like that, and I came back to my house and there was no one there to share it with... oh, it wouldn't make a lick of difference. The silence just amplifies the emotion, whatever it happens to be, until it's just buzzing under my skin. 

Like I've been trying to explain, it all comes back to being alone in that empty house. Once I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside completely. It just vanishes into thin air! And it is so incredibly frustrating, because even while I'm standing right there by the pantry, telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now, you don't need to do this,' my hands just keep reaching for more. My brain is giving the sensible orders, but my hands just absolutely refuse to listen. It’s like the euphoria itself just short-circuits my body the second the front door clicks shut and I'm by myself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's loss of control over eating is related to the emotional state or the fact of being alone
doctor.question: Do you think you would lose control over eating if you were alone but in a neutral emotional state, without feeling particularly sad, angry, or excited?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I take the first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense steps aside, and even while I'm telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands keep reaching for more.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is probing whether the loss of control over eating happens even in a neutral emotional state, which directly relates to the symptom of Loss of Control.

patient.answer:
Well doctor, it is funny you should ask that. Because just an ordinary Thursday... I think it was last Thursday, yes, because the garbage truck had just come by, and they always make such a racket out on the street. After they left, I was just doing my regular chores. Dusting the credenza my late husband Arthur built, folding some hand towels, nothing special at all. I wasn't sad, I wasn't happy, I certainly wasn't angry like I was with the electric company. I was just going about my business, feeling perfectly fine and normal, just a regular day. 

I went into the kitchen to have a little snack before my afternoon television programs came on. And I know I must sound like a broken record to you by now, I really do, but I have to tell you, it is the exact same story. It does not need a big, powerful emotion to start the whole dreadful thing. It is just the silence. The house gets so terribly quiet again after the chores are done. 

I know I have said this to you three times already, but it is the honest truth, the very moment I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it is like my good sense just completely steps aside. It just checks out! I will be standing right there by the counter, looking at a bag of pretzels or a box of crackers, and I am telling myself in my head, Belinda, stop now, you are not even upset, you are just bored, put the bag away. But my hands just keep reaching for more. They simply do not listen to a single word I am thinking. 

It is the most baffling thing in the world, doctor. You would think without the sadness or the excitement pushing me, I would be able to just put the food down and go read a magazine or do a crossword puzzle. But no, the quiet just settles in, and I lose all command all over again, even on a perfectly boring, ordinary afternoon. It is like my hands have a mind of their own, and they just keep going and going until everything is gone, no matter how I am feeling inside.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's loss of control over eating is related to the emotional state or the fact of being alone
doctor.question: Do you think you would lose control over eating if you were alone but feeling completely neutral emotionally?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I take the first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense steps aside, and even while I'm telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands keep reaching for more.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking again about losing control over eating, specifically in a neutral emotional state, which directly maps to the Loss of Control symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, did... did I not just answer that? Oh dear, perhaps I didn't explain it clearly enough, or maybe I just rambled on too much and lost the thread. My late husband, Arthur, always did say I could talk the ear off a brass monkey if you let me. But yes, to be perfectly clear, if I am completely and utterly neutral—just absolutely nothing going on in my head, maybe just standing at the sink watching the neighbor's cat, Mr. Whiskers, walk along the back fence—it still happens. It happens exactly the same way. 

Like I was just saying about doing my chores last Thursday, you really cannot find a more neutral feeling than folding hand towels. I wasn't feeling a single thing. But the house is still so terribly empty. And I know I keep repeating myself to you today, I really do, but it is the absolute gospel truth: once I take that first bite after the house is quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside. It just takes a holiday! And even while I'm standing right there in the middle of the kitchen, looking at whatever it is I've opened, and telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now, you aren't even upset, you don't even want this,' my hands just keep reaching for more. 

They just keep reaching and reaching, completely ignoring my brain. It is so terribly baffling, because if I'm not sad and I'm not happy, you would think I could just put the box back in the pantry and go water the African violets, wouldn't you? But I can't. The quiet just takes over, and my hands do whatever they please, even on the most boring, ordinary day you could possibly imagine.

doctor.intent: determine if loss of control over eating is related to emotional state or being alone
doctor.question: Do you think you would lose control over eating if you were in a crowded place, but still feeling sad or lonely?

target_item.name: Eating_Alone_Due_to_Embarrassment
target_item.manifestation: At bridge or church suppers I make a point of taking a modest little plate, then later after everyone has gone home I pull the leftovers out and eat in the kitchen where nobody can see me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the loss of control over eating would happen in a crowded place. This directly relates to the patient's symptom of eating alone due to embarrassment, where she restricts her eating in public (crowded places like church suppers) and binges when alone.

patient.answer:
Oh heavens, no. No, no, no, I could never do that. If I am around other people... oh, I could be feeling just absolutely heartbroken, missing Arthur so much my chest physically aches, or feeling completely invisible in a room full of people, but I would never, ever let myself go like that in front of a crowd. Never. 

It is... well, it is just too humiliating, doctor. People judge, you know they do, especially women my age. Take my Tuesday bridge club, for instance, or the potluck suppers we have down at the church. They always have those long tables set up with all sorts of wonderful casseroles and pies. But even if I am feeling incredibly lonely standing right there in that crowded church basement, I make a very special point of taking just a modest little plate. I will take a tiny scoop of ambrosia salad, maybe one small dinner roll, just like all the other ladies. I smile and I chat with the pastor's wife, and I make absolutely sure everyone sees how polite and little I am eating. I wouldn't dare let them see what I really want to do, I'd die of embarrassment! 

But then... well, then the supper is over, and everyone goes home. And they always insist on sending me back with plates of leftovers because they know I live alone. And the very minute I am back in my own house, and the door is locked, and there is nobody around to see me... that is when it happens. I take all those leftovers right out into the kitchen, and I pull back the aluminum foil, and I just eat everything right there where nobody can see me. Nobody can whisper about how much Belinda is putting on her plate, or give me those pitying little looks. So, no, to answer your question, it never happens in public. I have to be completely hidden away in my own kitchen for the control to slip, no matter how terribly sad I might be feeling out in the world.
